questions.q: What is a threat intelligence feed?
options: A one-time report an analyst writes after an incident is closed
A firewall configuration file that never changes
A list of employee names and their job titles
A continuously updated stream of confirmed-bad IOCs — malicious IPs, domains, and file hashes — from an external source
questions.explain: A feed packages thousands of already-confirmed IOCs so a SOC can consume them automatically instead of discovering each one from scratch.

questions.q: What is an ISAC, as a source of threat intelligence?
options: A type of firewall hardware appliance
An internal team that exists only within a single company
A commercial antivirus product sold only to governments
A sector-specific group where member organizations in the same industry pool what they're seeing
questions.explain: ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers) are sector-specific, non-profit groups, like one for the financial sector, where members share threat data on the theory that one target is often followed by another in the same industry.

questions.q: What does a Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP) actually do?
options: Writes phishing emails for a red team exercise
Replaces the need for any SIEM in the SOC
Only displays feed data on a dashboard with no further action
Ingests multiple feeds, deduplicates and scores them, and pushes the resulting blocklist to enforcement points like the firewall
questions.explain: A TIP automates the loop from feed data to actual enforcement, pushing blocklists out so a malicious IP is blocked before a human reviews it.

questions.q: What does 'enrichment' mean in the context of a SIEM alert?
options: Converting an alert into a different file format
Adding threat intelligence feed context to an alert so an analyst doesn't have to research it from scratch
Deleting low-priority alerts automatically
Increasing the storage capacity of the SIEM's database
questions.explain: Enrichment attaches feed context, such as how many other organizations have seen that same IP as malicious, so an analyst can act immediately.

questions.q: Why might a mature SOC blend feeds from commercial vendors, ISACs, and open-source projects rather than relying on just one?
options: Regulations require using exactly three feed sources
Commercial vendors never publish accurate data
Each source type tends to catch and publish different threats first
Open-source feeds are always more accurate than commercial ones
questions.explain: Vendors, ISACs, and open-source projects each have different visibility and speed advantages, so blending them catches more threats sooner than any single source alone.
